{"url":"https://tech-insider.org/tesla-car-company-auto-revenue-down-3-energy-down-16-2026/","title":"Tesla Auto Revenue Down 3%, Energy Down 16% [2026]","text":"October 23, 2026 10 min read
Tesla’s third-quarter 2026 report landed with a split verdict. Total revenue came in at $28.046 billion, essentially level with the $28.095 billion the company booked a year earlier. Underneath that flat headline, automotive revenue fell 3% to $20.560 billion and energy generation and storage revenue dropped 16% to $2.881 billion, according to Tesla’s financial materials. Coverage from Yahoo Finance, ABC13 Houston, The Motley Fool, Autoweek and AOL.com has since turned one question into the story of the week: is Tesla a car company, or something else?What Tesla Reported for Q3 2026Tesla Automotive Revenue Fell 3%: What Drove ItEnergy Generation and Storage Tumbled 16%: The Tariff Refund FactorServices and Other Rose to $4.605 BillionIs Tesla a Car Company? Reading the Revenue MixThe case that Tesla is still a car companyThe case that the label is changingProduction, Deliveries and 13.7 GWh: The Hardware Behind the RevenueWhy the Car Company Question Keeps Coming UpCompetitive Context: How Tesla’s Mix Stacks UpHistorical Context: Three Reporting Buckets, One Dominant LineMarket Impact: What Investors Should WeighWhat the Records Do Not ConfirmFour Predictions for Tesla’s Segment MixThe TakeawayFAQ: Tesla’s Q3 2026 Revenue MixRelated Coverage

The short answer from the numbers is that cars still carry the business. About 73% of Q3 revenue came from vehicles, and the energy division did not step in to fill the gap. We covered the raw delivery and storage figures in our Tesla Q3 earnings breakdown. This piece goes one level deeper and asks what the segment mix says about how investors should classify the company.

 What Tesla Reported for Q3 2026

Tesla splits its reporting into three categories: automotive, energy generation and storage, and services and other. All three moved in Q3, and not in the same direction. Total revenue slipped by roughly $49 million, a decline of about 0.2%. That tiny net change hides a $645 million drop in automotive, a $534 million drop in energy, and a $1.130 billion jump in services and other.

Tesla said the year-over-year revenue change reflected the decrease in energy generation and storage, which it tied partly to tariff-related customer refunds. The company also pointed to a lower average selling price on vehicles, lower regulatory-credit revenue and fewer vehicle deliveries. Those are Tesla’s own explanations, and the filing materials do not rank them by size.

SegmentQ3 2026 revenueQ3 2025 revenueDollar changeChangeTotal automotive$20.560B$21.205B-$0.645B-3%Energy generation and storage$2.881B$3.415B-$0.534B-16%Services and other$4.605B$3.475B+$1.130B+32.5% (our calculation)Total revenue$28.046B$28.095B-$0.049B-0.2% (our calculation)

Source for revenue figures: Tesla’s Q3 2026 financial results. Dollar changes and the services growth rate are our arithmetic on those figures.

Tesla Automotive Revenue Fell 3%: What Drove It

Tesla automotive revenue of $20.560 billion sits $645 million below the $21.205 billion from Q3 2025. A 3% slide is modest by the standards of a cyclical industry, but it matters here because automotive is still the foundation of the whole income statement. Every other line is small next to it.

Tesla named three automotive pressures in its explanation of the year-over-year change. Average selling price fell. Regulatory-credit revenue shrank. Vehicle deliveries came in lower. Each one cuts revenue through a different channel. Price hits every car sold, credits depend on policy and on how much other manufacturers lean on them, and volume is the simplest lever of the three.

Deliveries still topped 486,000 vehicles in the quarter, according to Tesla’s official Q3 update, against production of over 464,000. Going by those rounded figures, Tesla delivered roughly 22,000 more vehicles than it built, which means it pulled from inventory. That is a quiet but useful detail. A company can ship more than it makes for a quarter or two, but not indefinitely.

For investors weighing the 3% decline, the practical question is whether it marks a trough or a trend. One quarter cannot answer that. What it does show is that the car business is not growing fast enough to carry the stock on volume alone, and that pricing and credits are now meaningful drags rather than rounding errors.

Energy Generation and Storage Tumbled 16%: The Tariff Refund Factor

The energy line fell from $3.415 billion to $2.881 billion. That is the sharper percentage drop of the two big segments, and it undercuts the popular argument that storage is ready to shoulder more of Tesla’s weight. Tesla attributed part of the decline to tariff-related customer refunds, which is a very different cause from weak demand.

The deployment figure supports caution before reading the 16% as a demand signal. Tesla’s official Q3 update reported 13.7 GWh of energy-storage products deployed. Revenue and gigawatt-hours are different measures, and refunds can pull reported revenue down without reducing the amount of hardware shipped. The materials we reviewed do not give a year-ago GWh figure, so we will not claim a precise volume trend here. Our earlier piece on how storage hardware offset the auto decline covers the hardware angle in more detail.

What the data do not establish is how large the refund effect was, or whether it repeats next quarter. Tesla did not break the refund amount out in the materials we reviewed. Anyone modeling a rebound in Tesla energy generation and storage revenue is guessing at that number, and should say so.

Services and Other Rose to $4.605 Billion

The one segment that grew was services and other, which climbed from $3.475 billion to $4.605 billion. By our calculation that is a gain of about 32.5%, or $1.130 billion in a single year. It more than offset the energy decline in dollar terms and covered most of the automotive shortfall as well, which is why total revenue barely moved.

The category is a catch-all, and the official materials we have do not itemize what sits inside it. We will not guess at the components or their individual growth rates. What can be said is that services and other is now larger than energy generation and storage by a wide margin: $4.605 billion against $2.881 billion. A year ago the two were close, at $3.475 billion and $3.415 billion.

That crossover deserves more attention than it gets. When people ask whether Tesla is becoming an energy company, the data point somewhere else. The second-largest line is not batteries. It is the services and other bucket, and nobody outside Tesla can say precisely what is driving its growth from this disclosure alone.

Is Tesla a Car Company? Reading the Revenue Mix

Is Tesla a car company? On revenue share, yes. Automotive accounted for $20.560 billion of $28.046 billion, or about 73.3%. Services and other made up roughly 16.4%, and energy generation and storage about 10.3%. No reasonable reading of those percentages makes vehicles a minority business.

Shares are our calculations from Tesla’s reported segment revenue. Rounding means year-ago shares sum to 100.1%.

The case that Tesla is still a car company

Automotive is nearly three-quarters of revenue. Production of over 464,000 vehicles and deliveries of over 486,000 show the factories are running at scale. Energy fell, so the diversification story actually moved backward this quarter. The tariff-refund explanation softens that, but it does not erase the fact that energy revenue shrank.

Tesla Competitive Advantage

Tesla holds a $1.46 trillion market cap as of May 5, 2026, larger than the combined value of Toyota, BYD, GM, Ford, Mercedes-Benz, BMW, VW Group, Honda, Nissan, and several others.

The company delivered 358,023 EVs in Q1 2026, a 6.5% year-over-year jump. Rival BYD saw pure EV deliveries fall 25% in the same quarter.

Tesla’s Supercharger network includes over 70,000 stalls globally, and most major automakers including Ford, GM, and Mercedes have adopted the NACS standard.

The Model Y reached 118,531 global sales in March 2026, growing 35% year-over-year. Tesla’s Full Self-Driving software has logged 10.05 billion miles. Tesla’s vertical integration across batteries, software, and manufacturing keeps margins above legacy peers even as rivals expand their lineups.

Is Tesla a Long-Term Buy?

Tesla trades at a P/E ratio of 358 with a 52-week range of $271 to $498.83. The stock pulled back 26.2% from recent highs through April 2026.

Bulls point to robotaxi rollout, FSD approval in the EU expected in Q2 or Q3 2026, and energy storage growth. Bears flag declining auto margins, a global EV share of just 8.9%, and free cash flow turning negative due to AI and robotics spending.

Tesla suits investors comfortable with high volatility and a long horizon. Always consult a financial advisor before investing.

Tesla Future Market Share

U.S. EV market share for Tesla jumped from 41% in Q3 2025 to 59% in Q4 2025 after federal EV tax credits ended. Cox Automotive expects 45% full-year U.S. share for 2026.

Globally, Tesla holds 8.9% of all-electric sales as of March 2026, up from 8.2% in February. BYD leads at 17.1% but has lost share from 24.2% a year ago.

Rivian’s R2 launch and the upcoming R3 will pressure the Model Y in 2026 and 2027. Most legacy automakers are scaling back EV plans, with at least 18 cancelling or delaying programs.

Tesla’s long-term share trajectory depends on Cybercab production, FSD monetization, and the affordable Model Y Standard. Without new launches, share gains will fade once rivals recalibrate.

FAQs

Who are Tesla’s main competitors in 2026?
Tesla’s main competitors in 2026 are BYD, Toyota, General Motors, Ford, Volkswagen Group, Rivian, Lucid, NIO, XPeng, and Li Auto. BYD leads global EV sales at 17.1% share, while Tesla holds 59% of the U.S. EV market.

What is Tesla’s market cap compared to competitors?
Tesla’s market cap is $1.46 trillion as of May 5, 2026. That is larger than Toyota ($274.5B), BYD ($129.7B), GM ($87.6B), and Ford ($47.6B) combined, making Tesla the world’s most valuable automaker.

Who is Tesla’s biggest competitor globally?
BYD is Tesla’s biggest global competitor. BYD held 17.1% of global EV market share in March 2026 versus Tesla’s 8.9%. BYD does not sell in the U.S. due to trade restrictions, but dominates China and is expanding in Europe.

What makes Tesla different from its competitors?
Tesla differs through vertical integration, the Supercharger network with 70,000+ stalls, in-house FSD software with 10 billion logged miles, and the highest auto margins among major EV makers. The brand also benefits from Elon Musk’s profile.

How many direct competitors does Tesla have?

{"url":"https://www.iea.org/reports/global-ev-outlook-2026/executive-summary","title":"Executive summary - Global EV Outlook 2026 - IEA","text":"After another record year for EV sales, attention is turning to the impacts of the energy crisis for global car markets

 Electric car sales grew by 20% globally to exceed 20 million in 2025, meaning one-quarter of all new cars sold were electric. Europe saw the strongest growth among major electric vehicle (EV) markets, with electric car sales rising by more than 30% to reach 28% of total sales, following an increase in the stringency of the European Union’s CO2 standards for cars. China’s growth in electric car sales slowed slightly, in part due to a temporary halt to its trade-in scheme, but EVs still accounted for nearly 55% of all car sales. In the United States, electric car sales remained relatively stable at just under 10% of car sales, though the end of EV tax credits coincided with a drop in sales at the end of the year. Meanwhile, some emerging markets saw steep increases in electric car sales. In Southeast Asia, annual sales more than doubled to reach a sales share of nearly 20%, led by Viet Nam, Indonesia and Thailand. In Latin America, sales grew by 75%, led by Brazil and Mexico. More than 100 countries recorded electric car sales growth in 2025, and in one-third of these, they represented at least 10% of new car sales. Chinese automakers supplied 60% of global electric car sales in 2025, while European and North American automakers were each responsible for about 15% of global sales.                                                                                                                                         The ongoing energy crisis resulting from the conflict in the Middle East has brought reliance on oil imports into sharp focus in many countries. The road transport sector represents close to half of oil demand today, and policy responses to the long tail of the current crisis stand to shape the global car market for years to come. The oil crisis of the 1970s prompted the introduction of fuel efficiency standards, which resulted in close to a doubling of the fuel economy of conventional cars between 1975 and today, while during the Covid-19 pandemic, many countries introduced EV subsidies to boost uptake and support a broader economic recovery. In 2025, the global fleet of EVs avoided the consumption of around 1.7 million barrels of oil per day (mb/d), primarily in countries that have implemented fuel economy and CO2 standards, such as China and the European Union. Some countries in Southeast Asia – including Viet Nam, the largest EV market in the region – have already announced plans to expand or extend EV tax incentives as part of their response to the current energy crisis.

 Electric cars are poised to make up a greater share of total car sales in 2026

 The current high oil price environment is drawing consumer attention to the economic benefits of driving EVs. Electric cars generally have lower running costs than internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, mainly due to their higher efficiency. The recent rise in oil prices resulting from the conflict in the Middle East has further increased the cost savings associated with driving an EV. For example, based on average oil prices in April, the annual fuel cost savings associated with driving an EV in the European Union grew 35% compared to 2025 savings. For corporate fleets that travel long distances, the running cost savings can be several times larger than for the general consumer. Preliminary signs suggest EV sales are increasing in countries with supply concerns, or where fuel price increases have been particularly steep. However, the full implications of the current crisis will take time to register in the car market, due in part to the lag between vehicle orders and deliveries. For consumers in emerging economies with low rates of motorisation and high sensitivity to fuel prices, electric two- and three-wheelers look to be an attractive option – sales more than doubled year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026 in Southeast Asia, and grew more than 30% in India.Electric car sales broke records in a number of markets during the first quarter of 2026. Global sales, at around 3.9 million, were 8% lower than over the same period last year, primarily because of lower sales in China and the United States following key policy changes. However, this overall decline masks strong sales growth in many countries: in Europe, sales were up close to 30% year-on-year; countries in Asia Pacific excluding China saw year-on-year sales growth of 80%, and sales across Latin America were up by 75%. In March 2026, around 30 countries saw record-breaking monthly sales, and a further 60 countries recorded year-on-year sales growth. Preliminary April data shows that monthly electric car sales in China grew to a record high of over 60% of total car sales, even if year-to-date electric car sales remained lower than in 2025.  Global electric car sales are expected to grow to 23 million in 2026, representing 28% of total car sales. Europe is poised for the largest growth among major markets, with sales projected to increase by around 20% in 2026, such that one in three cars sold are electric. In China, electric car sales are set to grow across 2026, albeit at a slower rate than in previous years, to reach almost 60% of total car sales. Sales across Asia Pacific countries other than China are expected to grow by over 50%, while sales in Latin America are projected to rise by 45%. The wider economic impacts of the conflict in the Middle East might temper overall car sales. In many regions, however, there is upside potential to the 2026 EV forecast depending, in part, on how, when and which policies are enacted amid the current energy crisis. 

 Policies and affordability will continue to shape the EV outlook in key markets

 Even without any new policy announcements, the global fleet of EVs is projected to grow more than sixfold by 2035 from 2025 levels, to reach as many as 510 million, without counting electric two- or three-wheelers. The increasing cost-competitiveness of EVs, along with tighter CO2 and fuel economy standards, are poised to drive market growth, pushing up the share of EVs in global car sales to around 50% in 2035 in the IEA’s exploratory scenarios.1 By contrast, the share of ICE cars continues to shrink in all scenarios, and sales never return to their 2017 peak. In China, 70% of battery electric cars sold in 2025 were already cheaper than the average conventional car; in China’s small car segment, electric cars have already largely displaced sales of conventional cars. This price dynamic helps to push electric cars to exceed 90% of total car sales in China in 2035. In Europe, CO2 standards continue to drive sales of electric cars; in 2025, car manufacturers adjusted their pricing strategies and introduced more affordable EV models to comply with the new emissions targets. Enacting the proposed Automotive Package in the European Union would reduce the 2035 outlook nonetheless, but the sales share of electric cars still exceeds 90%.Policies and price dynamics are poised to drive EV sales in particular in Southeast Asia, where the share of electric car sales is projected to increase by up to three times by 2035. Imports of affordable electric cars from China have brought down prices and driven up EV sales in many emerging markets in recent years. For example, in Thailand, electric car prices have been on par with those of ICE cars for the past 2 years. In Indonesia, the average price premium for electric cars declined from over 50% in 2024 to around 40% in 2025. Some countries are looking to tighten import rules to support the development of domestic manufacturing, which may affect affordability in the future. Viet Nam is the only country in the region that has a sizeable domestic EV manufacturer offering EVs at prices comparable to those of ICE cars.  ·

 Compiled from the primary sources cited below

 Executive Summary
In 2025, the global EV market changed leadership. BYD sold 2.26 million battery-electric vehicles, surpassing Tesla's 1.64 million for the first time and becoming the world's largest BEV seller, with a gap of roughly 620,000 units. But the competition is about far more than sales volume. The two companies represent two very different business models: BYD is the executor of the present, while Tesla is the wager on the future. BYD's moat is vertical manufacturing integration and global market expansion. Tesla's bet is an AI ecosystem built around FSD, Robotaxi and the Optimus humanoid robot.[1][2][3]

I. Sales: BYD Takes the Lead, Tesla Rebounds in Q1 After Declines

2025 was Tesla's darkest year in the EV sales race. Sales fell 8.1% in China, 38.8% in Europe and 7.7% in the United States. All three core markets weakened at the same time, while 96.9% of Tesla's volume still depended on the Model 3 and Model Y, exposing a clear product-concentration problem.[6]
2026: Tesla Rebounds in Q1 and the Race Tightens Again
In 2026, the competitive pattern shifted again. In Q1 2026, Tesla delivered 358,000 BEVs, overtaking BYD's 310,000 BEVs and regaining the quarterly BEV sales crown after three quarters. Two factors drove the rebound: Tesla's Shanghai Gigafactory contributed more than 60% of global output and accelerated deliveries after supply-chain stabilization; meanwhile BYD faced a softer domestic market at the start of 2026 after pushing hard to meet its 2025 year-end targets. If plug-in hybrids are included, however, BYD still delivered roughly 700,000 vehicles globally in Q1 2026 and remained the overall plug-in leader.[7][8]
February 2026 marked another milestone: BYD's monthly export volume, 100,200 units, exceeded its domestic sales for the first time, rising 41.4% year over year and pushing the overseas share above 52%. That marked BYD's transition into a truly global company rather than a China-centered exporter.[9]

II. Financials: Two Profit Models, Scale and Premium

The key financial paradox: BYD has surpassed Tesla in revenue and net profit, yet Tesla's market capitalization remains roughly 7 to 14 times higher. The reason is not current automotive earnings. It is the market's extraordinary premium on the narrative that Tesla is an AI company rather than merely a car company. Robotaxi, Optimus and FSD subscriptions are priced as large options on future software economics.[3][15]

III. Core Technology: Two Different Paths to Intelligence
3.1 Battery Technology: LFP vs NMC
BYD centers its Blade Battery on lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, chemistry. The main advantages are safety, very low cost and long cycle life. In March 2026, BYD released its second-generation Blade Battery, claiming a 10% to 70% fast-charge time of only five minutes. More importantly, roughly 75% of BYD's core components are developed and produced in-house, creating one of the deepest vertical-integration systems in the global EV industry, from upstream lithium resources to cell manufacturing and vehicle battery-management systems.[5][16][17]
Tesla uses both nickel-manganese-cobalt and LFP batteries in models such as the Model 3 and Model Y. Its chemistry choices can provide higher energy density, but at higher cost and with different safety tradeoffs than LFP Blade batteries. Tesla's differentiation lies in its 4680 cylindrical battery roadmap and structural battery pack technology, which integrates the battery into the vehicle body to reduce cost. That system remains strategically important, although mass production has progressed more slowly than expected.[18]

BYD's strategy is democratization: give customers at every price point access to assisted-driving capability, then use the resulting data scale to create a feedback loop. Tesla insists on a premium subscription model and treats FSD as a core software-revenue engine. Without FSD revenue, Tesla's automotive profit pool would be much thinner.[19][23]
3.3 Charging Infrastructure: Mature Empire vs Late Comer
Tesla Supercharger network: Tesla has built the world's largest privately operated fast-charging network. By the end of 2025, it had 8,182 Supercharger stations and 77,682 stalls across 54 countries. In May 2026, Tesla passed 37,428 Supercharger stalls in the United States, accounting for 52% of US DC fast-charging stalls. With charging speeds up to 250 kW, Tesla still offers one of the smoothest charging experiences in the industry.[26][27][28]
BYD Flash Charging network: BYD is still early in infrastructure deployment, but its plan is more aggressive. By the end of 2026, BYD plans to build 20,000 flash-charging stations in China. Europe is targeted for 3,000 stations by 2027, with a global 2027 target of 6,000 stations. BYD claims five-minute charging for 300 kilometers of range. The global installed base is still roughly an order of magnitude behind Tesla's network, making charging infrastructure BYD's biggest short-term weakness in overseas expansion.[5]

The update, attributed to comments made around Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call, walks back years of looser promises about nationwide autonomy and replaces them with a narrower, fleet-managed rollout plan.What Changed: The New Robotaxi-Only Rollout PlanInside Tesla’s Earnings Call: What Elluswamy SaidGeofencing Explained: Why “Unsupervised” Doesn’t Mean EverywhereWhat Geofencing Actually RestrictsTesla’s Current Robotaxi FootprintWhat’s Confirmed and What Isn’t: A Fact CheckHow the Media Is Covering the StoryMarket Reaction: Wall Street’s Mixed ResponseA History of Shifting Full Self-Driving TimelinesCompetitive Context: Where Robotaxi Rivals StandWhat the Delay Means for Current FSD SubscribersThe Hardware and Compute Angle Behind the TimelineCapex, Capacity, and the Cost of Getting to Q2 2027Predictions: What to Watch Before Q2 2027Why This Framing Matters More Than the Date ItselfFrequently Asked QuestionsRelated Coverage

The news is rippling across tech and finance outlets today, October 22, 2026, with Electrek, Business Insider, BASENOR, Yahoo Finance, and Mezha.net all converging on the same basic shape of the story: unsupervised driving is coming, but it is coming later than owners hoped, and it is coming with strings attached. For a company that has spent a decade promising “full self-driving next year,” a concrete-sounding Q2 2027 date tied to Tesla’s own Robotaxi network is both a correction and a confession about how hard the last mile of autonomy really is.

Google · Preferred SourcesDon't miss new tech stories on GoogleAdd Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.Add nowWhat Changed: The New Robotaxi-Only Rollout Plan

The core change in Tesla’s messaging is the word “unsupervised.” For years, Tesla has sold Full Self-Driving as a supervised system: the car steers, brakes, and navigates, but a human must stay alert and ready to intervene. Tesla’s reported new target is to let specific customer-owned vehicles operate without that supervision requirement, starting around Q2 2027. According to the reporting, that is not the same as flipping a switch for every FSD-equipped car in the country.

Instead, the unsupervised capability would apply only to vehicles that have been added to Tesla’s managed Robotaxi network. That is a meaningful distinction. A Robotaxi-network car operates inside boundaries Tesla controls: specific routes, specific cities, and presumably specific weather and traffic conditions that Tesla’s own mapping and fleet-management systems have validated. A personally owned Model Y sitting in a driveway in a city without Robotaxi service would not qualify, at least not under the plan as currently described.

That nuance matters for anyone trying to figure out what this means for their own car. The practical effect, as reported, is that unsupervised FSD becomes something closer to an opt-in fleet program than a firmware update that unlocks hands-off driving everywhere the car already drives today under supervision.

Inside Tesla’s Earnings Call: What Elluswamy Said

The Q2 2027 timeline traces back to comments from Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s vice president of autonomous driving, during the company’s Q3 2026 earnings call. Elluswamy tied the schedule directly to the requirements a customer car would need to meet before it could join the Robotaxi fleet.

“The only additional requirement is to make sure that, for example, the customer Model Y can be part of the geofences and the fleet management that Tesla has for it to be fully autonomous.”Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla Vice President of Autonomous Driving, via The Verge

Elluswamy also put a rough date on when that integration could happen for the first wave of owners, framing it as an estimate rather than a locked commitment.

“We suspect sometime around Q2 of next year is when we can turn on customer vehicles to join the robotaxi fleet.”Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla Vice President of Autonomous Driving, via Tesla North

A third comment from the same call frames the technical side of the plan: Tesla intends to ship the same autonomy stack that runs its purpose-built Cybercab and Robotaxi fleet down to ordinary customer hardware, under the FSD version 15 label.

“Pretty soon we will be able to release the same software as Robotaxi as FSD 15 to customers.”Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla Vice President of Autonomous Driving, via BASENOR

Taken together, the three comments describe a single plan: unify the software between Robotaxi vehicles and customer cars, then gate access to unsupervised driving behind geofencing and fleet management rather than a blanket software unlock. It is worth noting that none of this comes from a dedicated press release or regulatory filing. It comes from an earnings call, which is why outlets covering the story are treating the Q2 2027 date as a target rather than a guarantee.

Geofencing Explained: Why “Unsupervised” Doesn’t Mean Everywhere

Geofencing is the practice of restricting an autonomous system’s operation to a defined, mapped area where the company running it has validated road conditions, signage, traffic patterns, and edge cases. Every major robotaxi operator uses some version of it, and Tesla’s reported plan leans on the same approach rather than trying to certify unsupervised driving for the open-ended variety of roads a privately owned car might encounter.

What Geofencing Actually Restricts

Under the reported plan, a customer vehicle would need to be formally added to Tesla’s fleet-management system, which tracks which cars are authorized to drive unsupervised and where. That is a software and administrative gate, not just a hardware one. Reports indicate that Tesla’s Robotaxi service currently sticks to low-speed routes and avoids highways and more complex driving environments, which suggests the initial unsupervised rollout for customer cars would inherit those same limits rather than immediately extending to highway driving or unmapped rural roads.

This is consistent with how Tesla has built out its FSD stack over the past several quarters. The company has leaned increasingly on its own mapping data, a shift covered in Tesla’s move to confirm its own FSD maps as its subscriber base passed 1.74 million. Geofenced, Tesla-mapped zones give the company a controlled environment to validate unsupervised behavior before loosening restrictions, which is exactly the kind of staged approach the Q2 2027 timeline implies.

Tesla’s Current Robotaxi Footprint

Reports describe Tesla’s Robotaxi service as currently operating in six U.S. metropolitan areas, though the available coverage does not establish an official, complete list of which specific neighborhoods or zones are included within each metro. That ambiguity is itself part of the story: Tesla has not published a definitive public map of exactly where unsupervised, customer-facing driving will be legal and functional once the Q2 2027 window arrives.

What is reported with more confidence is the character of the routes involved. The service leans on low-speed, mapped corridors and generally steers clear of highways and the kind of chaotic, multi-lane merges that remain the hardest problem in autonomous driving. That caution lines up with the broader rollout pattern Tesla has shown off in recent Robotaxi demonstration videos, which have focused on controlled, camera-friendly routes rather than open-ended driving challenges.

{"url":"https://electrek.co/2026/10/21/tesla-tsla-q3-2026-financial-results/","title":"Tesla (TSLA) releases Q3 2026 financial results: margins rebound, profit still falls","text":"Tesla (TSLA) released its financial results and shareholders’ letter for the third quarter (Q3) 2026 after market close today. We’re updating this post with all the details from the financial results, shareholders’ letter, and the conference call later tonight.

The earnings call with management is scheduled for 5:30 p.m. ET.

Tesla Q3 2026 earnings expectations

Wall Street came into the report expecting a flat quarter. The FactSet consensus, as displayed on Estimize, called for $28.06 billion in revenue, essentially unchanged from the $28.1 billion Tesla posted in Q3 2025 and a bit below the $28.24 billion it reported last quarter.

Profit expectations were lower. Analysts were looking for non-GAAP earnings of $0.45 per share, down 10% from $0.50 a year ago. The Estimize crowd was slightly more bullish at $28.36 billion and $0.48.

We already had the volume numbers. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in Q3, down 2.1% year-over-year but well ahead of the 461,974 consensus, while producing only 464,391. It also deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage, up from 12.5 GWh a year ago but short of the roughly 15.9 GWh analysts expected. For the full setup, see our Q3 2026 earnings preview.

So the question was never volume. It was whether Tesla could stop the profit slide after Q2, when operating margin fell to 1.4% and EPS missed the consensus by 20 cents.

Tesla Q3 2026 financial results

After the market closed today, Tesla released its financial results for the third quarter and reported $28.05 billion in revenue, flat from a year ago and in line with the $28.06 billion Wall Street expected. Non-GAAP earnings came in at $0.48 per share, beating the $0.45 consensus but down 4% from $0.50 a year ago.

It’s a better quarter than Q2, but the trend hasn’t changed. Margins recovered, with auto gross margin excluding credits back above 18%, yet operating income still fell 56% year-over-year as spending on AI and Optimus grew faster than gross profit. On a GAAP basis, net income dropped 43% to $787 million, or $0.22 per share.

Total gross margin was 19.6%, up 160 basis points from 18.0% a year ago and well above the 16.8% Tesla posted in Q2. Operating income fell 56% to $718 million, for an operating margin of 2.6%, compared with 5.8% a year ago and 1.4% last quarter.

Operating expenses came in at $4.78 billion, up 39% year-over-year. Research and development alone jumped 69% to $2.76 billion as Tesla spends on what it now calls “Super Intelligence” (SI), Optimus, and the Cybercab. Stock-based compensation, which includes the 2025 CEO pay package, hit $1.17 billion, up from $663 million a year ago.

Capital spending was $4.73 billion, more than double the $2.25 billion of a year ago, and free cash flow came in at $1.53 billion, compared with $3.99 billion a year ago and negative $1.09 billion in Q2. Tesla ended the quarter with $45.4 billion in cash and investments. GAAP net income included a $288 million unrealized gain on Tesla’s bitcoin holdings, partly offset by a $142 million unrealized loss on its SpaceX equity investment.

That puts Tesla’s capex at $13.01 billion through the first nine months of 2026, only about half of the “more than $25 billion” management guided for the year. To hit that number, Tesla would need to spend roughly $12 billion in Q4 alone, more than double its biggest quarter so far. The Q3 letter doesn’t update the guidance, and capex actually fell sequentially from $5.79 billion in Q2. So either Q4 spending explodes, or the 2026 plan is quietly slipping into 2027. The lower spending also flatters this quarter’s positive free cash flow.

Tesla’s auto margin without credits

The number we watch first is automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits, now that the credit market has mostly dried up. It came in at 18.1% this quarter, up from 16.3% in Q2 and 15.4% a year ago, though still below the 19.2% of Q1, when Tesla got help from warranty and tariff one-time benefits. Tesla credits a better regional and product mix and more FSD subscription revenue, partly offset by lower average selling prices.

Regulatory credits brought in just $113 million, down 73% from $417 million a year ago and below the $146 million in Q2. That line isn’t coming back now that automakers no longer pay federal fuel-economy penalties.

Energy was the weak spot on revenue. Energy generation and storage revenue fell 16% to $2.88 billion, which Tesla partly blames on tariff-related customer refunds, even though deployments rose 10% to 13.7 GWh. The segment’s gross margin jumped to 33% from 20% in Q2, but energy gross profit still slipped to $954 million from $1.07 billion a year ago.

Services and other was the bright spot. Revenue grew 33% to $4.61 billion, and Tesla says gross profit hit a record $734 million on charging, insurance and parts sales.

Tesla blames batteries, not demand

Tesla says “battery availability continued to be the limiting factor in increasing auto volumes in the quarter,” and that it ended Q3 with “the largest backlog for our passenger vehicles in four years.”

That’s a new explanation for flat sales. Deliveries were still down 2% year-over-year, “other models” (Cybertruck, Semi, Model S and X) fell 48%, and Tesla delivered 22,141 more cars than it built, bringing inventory down to 11 days of supply from 15 in Q2. But average selling prices fell again, which isn’t usually what a supply-constrained automaker does.

On autonomy, Tesla says active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million, up 67%, though that count includes upfront purchases, as defined in Musk’s 2025 pay package. Its Robotaxi service reached nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles by the end of the quarter, a month after Cybercab joined the Austin fleet.

arguments.summary: Tesla remains ~73% a car company by revenue (Q3 2026: $28.05B total, flat YoY; automotive $20.56B -3%, energy $2.88B -16%, services & other $4.61B +32.5%), but the investment case now rests on FSD/Robotaxi/Optimus optionality, not car volume. Competitive position is strong in the US (59% EV share Q4 2025) but weak globally (8.9% BEV share vs BYD's 17.1%); BYD overtook Tesla in 2025 on BEV volume, revenue and net profit. Core EV market is large (23M units forecast 2026) but decelerating, while autonomy monetization has slipped to 2027 and is geofenced.
findings: Tesla is still a car company by revenue: Q3 2026 automotive revenue of $20.56B was ~73% of the $28.05B total; energy generation & storage was $2.88B (-16% YoY) and services & other rose to $4.61B (+32.5%), now the second-largest segment [S6].
Total Q3 2026 revenue was essentially flat YoY ($28.046B vs $28.095B), with automotive down 3% and energy down 16% (partly tariff-related customer refunds), offset by the services & other jump [S6].
Q3 2026 hardware: vehicle deliveries topped 486,000 against production of over 464,000, and energy storage deployments reached 13.7 GWh [S6].

Profitability improved despite flat revenue: automotive gross margin ex-regulatory-credits rose to 18.1% (from 16.3%), energy gross margin to 33.1% (from 20.4%), with $1.5B free cash flow and $45B+ cash on hand [S5].
FSD monetization is scaling: 1.7M+ paid FSD customers globally with subscriptions now 50% of the base, and over 75% of North American deliveries included a paid FSD sign-up [S5].

Globally, BYD leads Tesla: BYD held 17.1% of global EV sales (March 2026) versus Tesla's 8.9%, while Tesla holds a dominant 59% share of the US EV market (Q4 2025, up from 41% after federal EV tax credits ended) [S10].

BYD overtook Tesla in 2025 on multiple measures: BEV sales 2.26M vs 1.64M, revenue ~$107.2B vs $94.8B, and net profit ~$4.7B vs $3.8B (GAAP); Tesla's 2025 sales fell in the US (-7.7%), Europe (-38.8%) and China (-8.1%) [S9].
Tesla's volume is highly concentrated: 96.9% of 2025 deliveries were Model 3/Y, a product-concentration risk; Q1 2026 showed a rebound with Tesla's 358k BEVs outpacing BYD's 310k BEVs [S9].

Core EV market is large but growth is slowing: global EV sales exceeded 20M in 2025 (~25% of new cars), forecast at 23M in 2026 (~28% of sales); Q1 2026 global sales of ~3.9M were down 8% YoY due to policy changes in the US and China, though Europe grew ~30% [S7].
The US EV market remains small (~10% of car sales in 2025) and lost its federal tax credit at end-2025, a headwind; the Middle East oil crisis is a demand tailwind for EVs and energy storage [S7].

Adjacent autonomy/robotics optionality is real but slipping: robotaxi unsupervised miles grew 8x QoQ, but unsupervised FSD on customer-owned cars was pushed to Q2 2027 and limited to geofenced Robotaxi zones; robotaxi revenue is expected to be 'noticeable' only in Q2 2027 [S5][S8].

Capital intensity is rising: 2026 capex guidance raised to ~$20B, and Tesla's Terafab chip ambitions could require $100B+ long-term, while Optimus mass production (20k/week) is at least a year away with reliability targets set for end-2027 [S5].
arguments.counter_evidence: Against a Buy: (1) the core car business is not growing — Q3 2026 revenue flat, auto -3% and energy -16% [S6]; (2) Tesla lost global EV leadership to BYD in 2025 and holds only 8.9% global BEV share, with 2025 sales down in all three core markets and 96.9% of volume in Model 3/Y [S9][S10]; (3) the autonomy thesis has been walked back — unsupervised FSD is delayed to Q2 2027 and geofenced to Robotaxi zones, so robotaxi revenue is not material until 2027 [S8][S5]; (4) valuation is extreme (P/E ~358) while capex is escalating (~$20B in 2026, Terafab up to $100B+), pressuring free cash flow [S10][S5].
gaps: Conflicting Q3 2026 delivery figures across secondary sources (TradingKey ~408,000 vs Tech Insider >486,000); the primary Q3 2026 filing would resolve this.
Energy segment tariff-refund amount not disclosed — the 16% energy revenue decline is partly non-recurring, so a rebound cannot be modeled with confidence.
Composition of 'services and other' ($4.61B, +32.5%) is not itemized in the sources retrieved.
Specific trade-policy details (US Section 301 tariffs, EU price floor) were not retrieved from primary policy sources this run.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## E1 (Market Analyst): Tesla (TSLA) — business, competitors, market size and news/regulation (Buy/Sell support, late Oct 2026)
Tesla remains ~73% a car company by revenue (Q3 2026: $28.05B total, flat YoY; automotive $20.56B -3%, energy $2.88B -16%, services & other $4.61B +32.5%), but the investment case now rests on FSD/Robotaxi/Optimus optionality, not car volume. Competitive position is strong in the US (59% EV share Q4 2025) but weak globally (8.9% BEV share vs BYD's 17.1%); BYD overtook Tesla in 2025 on BEV volume, revenue and net profit. Core EV market is large (23M units forecast 2026) but decelerating, while autonomy monetization has slipped to 2027 and is geofenced.
Findings:
- Tesla is still a car company by revenue: Q3 2026 automotive revenue of $20.56B was ~73% of the $28.05B total; energy generation & storage was $2.88B (-16% YoY) and services & other rose to $4.61B (+32.5%), now the second-largest segment [S6].
- Total Q3 2026 revenue was essentially flat YoY ($28.046B vs $28.095B), with automotive down 3% and energy down 16% (partly tariff-related customer refunds), offset by the services & other jump [S6].
- Q3 2026 hardware: vehicle deliveries topped 486,000 against production of over 464,000, and energy storage deployments reached 13.7 GWh [S6].
- Profitability improved despite flat revenue: automotive gross margin ex-regulatory-credits rose to 18.1% (from 16.3%), energy gross margin to 33.1% (from 20.4%), with $1.5B free cash flow and $45B+ cash on hand [S5].
- FSD monetization is scaling: 1.7M+ paid FSD customers globally with subscriptions now 50% of the base, and over 75% of North American deliveries included a paid FSD sign-up [S5].
- Globally, BYD leads Tesla: BYD held 17.1% of global EV sales (March 2026) versus Tesla's 8.9%, while Tesla holds a dominant 59% share of the US EV market (Q4 2025, up from 41% after federal EV tax credits ended) [S10].
- BYD overtook Tesla in 2025 on multiple measures: BEV sales 2.26M vs 1.64M, revenue ~$107.2B vs $94.8B, and net profit ~$4.7B vs $3.8B (GAAP); Tesla's 2025 sales fell in the US (-7.7%), Europe (-38.8%) and China (-8.1%) [S9].
- Tesla's volume is highly concentrated: 96.9% of 2025 deliveries were Model 3/Y, a product-concentration risk; Q1 2026 showed a rebound with Tesla's 358k BEVs outpacing BYD's 310k BEVs [S9].
- Core EV market is large but growth is slowing: global EV sales exceeded 20M in 2025 (~25% of new cars), forecast at 23M in 2026 (~28% of sales); Q1 2026 global sales of ~3.9M were down 8% YoY due to policy changes in the US and China, though Europe grew ~30% [S7].
- The US EV market remains small (~10% of car sales in 2025) and lost its federal tax credit at end-2025, a headwind; the Middle East oil crisis is a demand tailwind for EVs and energy storage [S7].
- Adjacent autonomy/robotics optionality is real but slipping: robotaxi unsupervised miles grew 8x QoQ, but unsupervised FSD on customer-owned cars was pushed to Q2 2027 and limited to geofenced Robotaxi zones; robotaxi revenue is expected to be 'noticeable' only in Q2 2027 [S5][S8].
- Capital intensity is rising: 2026 capex guidance raised to ~$20B, and Tesla's Terafab chip ambitions could require $100B+ long-term, while Optimus mass production (20k/week) is at least a year away with reliability targets set for end-2027 [S5].
Counter-evidence: Against a Buy: (1) the core car business is not growing — Q3 2026 revenue flat, auto -3% and energy -16% [S6]; (2) Tesla lost global EV leadership to BYD in 2025 and holds only 8.9% global BEV share, with 2025 sales down in all three core markets and 96.9% of volume in Model 3/Y [S9][S10]; (3) the autonomy thesis has been walked back — unsupervised FSD is delayed to Q2 2027 and geofenced to Robotaxi zones, so robotaxi revenue is not material until 2027 [S8][S5]; (4) valuation is extreme (P/E ~358) while capex is escalating (~$20B in 2026, Terafab up to $100B+), pressuring free cash flow [S10][S5].
Gaps: Conflicting Q3 2026 delivery figures across secondary sources (TradingKey ~408,000 vs Tech Insider >486,000); the primary Q3 2026 filing would resolve this.; Energy segment tariff-refund amount not disclosed — the 16% energy revenue decline is partly non-recurring, so a rebound cannot be modeled with confidence.; Composition of 'services and other' ($4.61B, +32.5%) is not itemized in the sources retrieved.; Specific trade-policy details (US Section 301 tariffs, EU price floor) were not retrieved from primary policy sources this run.; Regulatory timing for EU-wide and China FSD approvals is outside Tesla's control and unverified.

{"url":"https://bydtoday.com/china-robotaxi-commercial-scale-2026/","title":"China Robotaxi 2026: Baidu, Pony.ai, WeRide and Commercial Scale","text":"Quick Answer: China has paid, fully driverless robotaxi services, but only inside company- and city-approved operating zones. Baidu Apollo Go reported 3.2 million driverless rides in Q1 2026 and more than 22 million cumulatively. Pony.ai reported a fleet above 1,700 and RMB 59.1 million of Q1 robotaxi revenue; WeRide reported about 1,000 robotaxis in China. None of this means nationwide L4 approval or industry-wide profitability.
Last verified: July 17, 2026. Company scale uses Baidu, Pony.ai and WeRide’s latest Q1 2026 disclosures; city status uses national and local government sources. Targets are labeled separately from achieved figures.
Page role: This is BYDToday’s single evergreen Owner for the China robotaxi ecosystem. It updates Post 1418 in place and does not create a second URL. The June 2026 global robotaxi ranking remains dated supporting coverage, not the market Owner.
What counts as a commercial robotaxi in China?
A robotaxi is an autonomous ride-hailing vehicle operating within a defined operational design domain, or ODD. The ODD can limit roads, hours, weather, speed, passenger rules and pickup points. “Fully driverless” normally means no safety operator is sitting in the vehicle during the approved service. It does not mean the vehicle can drive everywhere, in every condition, without an operations center or regulatory constraints.
China does not have one blanket licence that turns every L4 test car into a nationwide taxi. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology says its intelligent connected-vehicle access and road-use pilot has multiple stages. Selection into the pilot is not itself product approval or permission to drive on public roads. A vehicle that passes product access still needs registration, a limited road-use area and, when it carries passengers for payment, the relevant transport-operation qualifications.
Local systems add another layer. Wuhan distinguishes road testing, demonstration application and a commercial pilot that may charge passengers. Shanghai describes separate permits for testing, robotaxi service with an onboard safety officer and fully commercial operation. This is why a company can truthfully say it is “commercial” in one zone while remaining in testing or demonstration elsewhere.

Baidu Apollo Go: the ride-volume leader
Baidu’s Q1 2026 results provide the clearest disclosed ride scale. Apollo Go delivered 3.2 million fully driverless operational rides during the quarter, with weekly rides peaking above 350,000 in March. Rides grew more than 120% year over year, and cumulative public rides exceeded 22 million by April. By May, Baidu said Apollo Go had reached 27 cities globally and accumulated more than 330 million autonomous kilometres, including over 220 million fully driverless kilometres.
Those are company-reported operational metrics. They should not be converted into revenue by multiplying rides by an assumed fare. Baidu does not publish Apollo Go as a standalone financial segment, so its revenue, operating cost, vehicle utilisation and profitability cannot be derived reliably from the group accounts. The accurate conclusion is scale leadership in disclosed rides—not proven nationwide profit.
Baidu’s own business overview adds two useful boundaries. It says Apollo Go’s mainland China operations had become fully driverless by February 2025, meaning its listed mainland services no longer relied on an onboard safety operator inside the approved operating domains. It also says the sixth-generation RT6, a vehicle designed for autonomous ride-hailing rather than ordinary retail ownership, entered operation in October 2024. A purpose-built vehicle can improve passenger space, serviceability and fleet integration, but it does not remove the need for local permits, depot operations, charging, cleaning, maintenance or remote support.
Pony.ai: the clearest robotaxi revenue disclosure
Pony.ai’s Q1 2026 filing is more detailed on economics. It reported US$8.6 million, or RMB 59.1 million, of robotaxi services revenue, up 395.4% year over year. Fare-charging revenue rose 456.5%. The company said its robotaxi fleet exceeded 1,700; a footnote specified 1,776 vehicles produced as of May 24. It also reported a Q1 net loss of US$53.5 million, or RMB 369.1 million, for the whole company.
Pony said its seventh-generation fleet had achieved city-wide vehicle-level unit-economics breakeven in Guangzhou and Shenzhen in late 2025. That is a narrower measure than corporate profitability: it does not include every central R&D, administrative, expansion or financing cost. Its target of more than 3,500 robotaxis in over 20 cities by the end of 2026 and a sub-RMB 230,000 total vehicle cost by mid-2027 are useful milestones, but they remain targets rather than completed outcomes.
WeRide: higher disclosed utilisation, mixed revenue lines
WeRide reported about 1,300 robotaxis globally and about 1,000 in China at April 30, 2026. During Q1, average daily orders per vehicle exceeded 17 and reached 28 in peak periods. The company reported RMB 114.1 million of total revenue and an RMB 431.0 million operating loss. Product revenue of RMB 20.5 million included robotaxi and other L4 vehicle sales, while service revenue included intelligent-data and ADAS services.
The company’s utilisation disclosure is valuable, but the accounting scope matters. Total revenue is not robotaxi fare revenue, and product revenue is not the same as operating rides. WeRide’s partnerships with local fleet operators and platforms such as Uber point toward a more asset-light route overseas, while its China fleet remains an important base for deployment and user adoption.

WeRide displayed its production-ready Robotaxi GXR at NVIDIA GTC 2026. Image: WeRide official release.

{"url":"https://www.mobileye.com/news/mobileye-to-establish-vertically-integrated-robotaxi-business/","title":"Mobileye to establish vertically integrated robotaxi business | Mobileye News","text":"JERUSALEM, June 16, 2026 — Mobileye today announced plans to expand its robotaxi activities beyond supplying self-driving technology and into full ownership of an autonomous ride-hailing business. Rather, Mobileye views direct robotaxi operations as a complementary path to market that can accelerate deployment, generate operational learnings, and further demonstrate the capabilities of the Mobileye Drive platform at scale. The company expects its customer-driven and directly operated robotaxi programs to advance in parallel.Mobileye is planning to prepare an initial fleet of about 100 vehicles targeted for deployment in a major metropolitan U.S. market beginning in 2027. {"url":"https://electrek.co/2026/10/21/tesla-unsupervised-fsd-q2-2027-robotaxi-fleet/","title":"Tesla pushes unsupervised FSD to Q2 2027, and only inside Robotaxi zones","text":"Tesla now says unsupervised “Full Self-Driving” in customer-owned cars will arrive in Q2 2027. It’s the latest date on a promise Elon Musk has been making to FSD buyers for the better part of a decade.

But there’s a catch. On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call today, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy described it as owners adding their own vehicles to Tesla’s managed Robotaxi fleet, not owners getting a car that drives them anywhere they want to go.

“When can we anticipate FSD unsupervised in customer cars?” was one of the top retail shareholder questions submitted for the call, backed by about 1.1 million shares, as we noted in our Tesla Q3 2026 earnings preview.

Elluswamy’s answer was Q2 2027. And the way he framed it, step one isn’t a software update that lets you climb into the back of your Model Y and sleep while it drives you to your destination – what Elon Musk sold to customers since 2016. It’s Tesla letting owners put their cars into its own Robotaxi network, where Tesla runs the operation.

So an owner’s car would only drive itself unsupervised where Tesla’s Robotaxi already operates.

Those zones are small

Tesla’s Robotaxi service runs in six US metros right now, and most of the service areas cover small slices of those cities. When Tesla mapped its Miami Robotaxi zone, it covered mostly West Miami and a strip toward Doral and Sweetwater. Orlando and Tampa launched in July with similarly small geofences.

Inside those zones, the service sticks to low-speed routes, largely stays off highways, and avoids the harder parts of town. In the Bay Area, it isn’t unsupervised at all. California rules still require a safety driver in every car because Tesla doesn’t want to release data to the California DMV, which it has to do beyond a level 2 autonomous system.

The fleet is small too. Tesla says Robotaxi reached nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles by the end of Q3, a month after Cybercab joined the Austin fleet, according to Tesla’s Q3 2026 results. Third-party tracking this spring showed the number of fully driverless Teslas on the road in the dozens, nowhere near the hundreds of thousands Musk had talked about. Waymo, meanwhile, was already in both Orlando and Tampa before Tesla showed up, and it has over 3 million miles.

The promise vs. the product

That’s not what Tesla sold. For years, the pitch to FSD buyers was a car that would eventually drive itself anywhere through a software update.

Musk told investors in July 2025 that unsupervised FSD would be available “for unsupervised personal use by the end of this year in certain geographies.” A year earlier, he said he’d be “surprised” if Tesla didn’t have unsupervised self-driving the following year. And HW3 owners who bought FSD have already been told their computers can’t run unsupervised FSD at all, with no clear upgrade plan.

Now the target is Q2 2027, and the product is narrower: your car joins Tesla’s fleet, in Tesla’s zones, on Tesla’s terms.

Electrek’s Take

	If you can believe it. Believing a Tesla FSD timeline is a fool’s errand at this point, and I don’t see any reason to treat Q2 2027 differently from every other date Tesla has given since 2019.

This moves the goalpost from “your car drives you anywhere while you sleep” to “your car can work as a Robotaxi inside a small geofence that Tesla controls.” No highway road trips. No driving you home from the airport across town. No unsupervised commute unless you happen to live and work inside one of the zones.

It’s the goalpost moving of all goalpost moving.If one thing was clear from the call, Tesla has no idea when it will actually happen. They are just guessing. Ashok again reiterated that safety is the bottleneck, which is why Tesla limits itself to low-speed roads and harder environments. He guesses that those safety issues will be fixed by next year, but he doesn’t know.

{"url":"https://electrek.co/2026/10/22/tesla-cuts-2026-capex-guidance-q3-cash-flow/","title":"Tesla (TSLA) quietly cuts 2026 capex guidance to $20B","text":"Tesla has lowered its 2026 capital spending forecast. In its Q3 10-Q, the company now says it expects capital expenditures “to be in excess of $20 billion in 2026,” down from the “more than $25 billion” it had guided since April.

The change was in the 10-Q Tesla filed Wednesday, not in the shareholder letter it released the same day. And it lands in a quarter where Tesla reported $1.53 billion of positive free cash flow, a number that depends a lot on timing.

Tesla’s 2026 capex guidance keeps moving

Tesla started 2026 guiding to about $20 billion in capex. In April, it raised that to more than $25 billion, and in July, CFO Vaibhav Taneja reiterated the figure while Elon Musk called 2026 a “massive capex year.”

Now it’s back to “in excess of $20 billion.”

Tesla has spent $13.01 billion so far this year: $2.49 billion in Q1, $5.79 billion in Q2 and $4.73 billion in Q3. Hitting $25 billion would have required about $12 billion in Q4 alone, more than double its biggest quarter. The new floor only requires about $7 billion.

The 10-Q says 2026 spending is “driven by our SI initiatives, including investments in compute infrastructure and data centers,” along with factory ramps and Tesla’s fleet of “company-operated SI-enabled assets.”

There’s a catch in the cash numbers, though. Tesla had $3.67 billion of equipment and construction spending sitting in liabilities at the end of September, meaning it was booked but not yet paid. That’s up from $2.63 billion at the end of June and $1.63 billion a year ago. So Tesla’s actual spending is running ahead of the cash capex it reports.

Where Tesla’s Q3 free cash flow came from

Tesla reported $6.26 billion in operating cash flow and $1.53 billion in free cash flow after capex. Here’s how it got there:

Q3 2026AmountNet income$0.80BDepreciation, amortization and impairment+$1.85BStock-based compensation+$1.17BOther non-cash items (FX, taxes, bitcoin, SpaceX)-$0.15BChanges in working capital+$2.59BOperating cash flow$6.26BCapital expenditures-$4.73BFree cash flow$1.53B

Depreciation and stock compensation are normal add-backs. They reduce profit without using cash.

The working capital line is the one to watch. Without that $2.59 billion, Tesla’s free cash flow would have been about negative $1.06 billion.

Most of it came from bills Tesla hasn’t paid yet. Accounts payable rose $1.92 billion in the quarter and accrued liabilities rose $1.95 billion, including $722 million more in “accrued purchases,” goods Tesla received but hadn’t been invoiced for.

Another $1.26 billion came from deferred revenue, mostly energy storage. Tesla’s energy deferred revenue jumped to $3.30 billion from $2.31 billion. But not all of that is cash. Tesla disclosed that it billed SpaceX $588 million for Megapacks “that have not been delivered,” which SpaceX hadn’t paid at quarter-end. That amount sits in both deferred revenue and accounts receivable, which rose $565 million.

Those gains were partly offset by a $1.82 billion increase in prepaid expenses and other assets, and a small inventory build.

If you also count the $1.03 billion increase in unpaid capex, Tesla’s free cash flow on an “as spent” basis was closer to $500 million.

Tesla’s borrowing plans

The capex cut comes a month after Tesla signed $30 billion of new credit facilities. The 10-Q details them: a $20 billion delayed-draw term loan maturing in 2029, and $10 billion of revolving credit replacing a $5 billion facility. Tesla hadn’t drawn on either at quarter-end, and it had $45.4 billion in cash and investments.

Electrek’s Take

	None of this is improper in today’s accounting standards, which we can argue are pretty awful. Paying suppliers later, collecting deposits, and booking capex when it’s incurred are all somewhat normal accounting, and Tesla disclosed them. But they explain why the “$1.5 billion of free cash flow” headline from Wednesday’s results says less about the business than it seems.

Underneath, Tesla made $718 million of operating income, less than its $1.17 billion in stock compensation, and before working capital, it burned cash. The timing items that helped this quarter will reverse when the invoices come due and the Megapacks ship.

The capex cut is the more interesting signal. Six months ago, Tesla was telling investors 2026 would be a massive spending year to build out AI compute, Optimus and Cybercab. Now it’s lowering the target in its 10-Q instead of the shareholder letter, while lining up $30 billion of debt. Either projects are slipping into 2027, or Tesla is spending less to protect its cash. Tesla should say which.

 BUSINESS / STOCK & DELIVERIES

 Tesla lowered its full-year 2026 capital spending guidance to $20 billion from $25 billion on its Q3 earnings call on Oct. 21, 2026, saying it would fund spending primarily from operating cash flow. Q3 capex was $4.732 billion and free cash flow was a positive $1.531 billion.
 By the Tesla News Wire staff · Edited by Seamus McKenna · October 21, 2026 · 2 min read
 Photo: Ministério Das Comunicações / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0 (cropped, resized). File photo from May 2022.
 Tesla now plans to spend $5 billion less this year than it said before. On its Q3 2026 earnings call on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, Tesla updated its full-year capital expenditure guidance to $20 billion, down from $25 billion, Yahoo Finance reported. Tesla's 10-Q, filed the same day, words it as capex "in excess of $20 billion in 2026," down from "more than $25 billion" (more from the 10-Q). CFO Vaibhav Taneja said the company is "managing our capital deployment efficiently" and plans to fund capex "primarily from our cash flows from operations."
The quarter's cash numbers (Tesla Q3 2026 update)

Capital expenditures: $4.732 billion (Q2 2026: $5.789 billion; Q3 2025: $2.248 billion)
Operating cash flow: $6.263 billion
Free cash flow: $1.531 billion, after negative $1.092 billion in Q2 2026
Cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments: $45.447 billion, up $1.9 billion in the quarter

Yahoo Finance said analysts had estimated Q3 capex of $7.96 billion and free cash flow of negative $4.92 billion. CNBC noted free cash flow was still down 62% from a year earlier.
What Musk said about future spending
"I think capex is actually ending up being a little lower than we anticipated, but we'll start to become more meaningful next year. And then noticeable in the tens of billions in '28," Musk said on the call, according to Yahoo Finance. Yahoo said the money is going to Optimus production lines, AI compute, the Cybercab ramp and the Terafab chip plant Tesla is building with SpaceX.

# Tesla (TSLA): investment memo
Rating: Sell
Data as of: 2026-10-28

## Executive summary
Sell. Tesla's core automotive business has stopped growing and its profitability has collapsed: GAAP net income fell from $15.0B (FY2023) to $3.79B (FY2025) [S2][S3][S4], and Q3 2026 net income of $787M was down 43% year-over-year on flat revenue [S12][S13]. The autonomy/robotaxi thesis that carries the valuation has slipped, and Tesla now trails the only scaled Western operator: unsupervised FSD is delayed to Q2 2027 and confined to geofenced zones, while Waymo is already running ~500k paid rides a week [S8][S16][S21]. The market still prices this at ~$1.61T, roughly 500x trailing earnings [S1][S12][S14]. The balance sheet is strong, so this is not a distress call; the valuation embeds growth and margins the business is not delivering. Global EV sales exceeded 20M in 2025 and are forecast at ~23M for 2026, but Q1 2026 was down 8% YoY on US and China policy shifts [S7].

Autonomy benchmark — Tesla is behind the only scaled Western operator. Waymo runs ~3,000 robotaxis and ~500k paid rides/week (~4M rider-only miles/week) across 11 US cities, and is targeting ~1M rides/week plus Tokyo and London by end-2026 [S16]. Baidu Apollo Go leads on disclosed ride volume but is China-only and geofenced: 3.2M fully driverless rides in Q1 2026, >22M cumulative, 27 cities, no standalone economics disclosed [S17]. Cruise exited (GM ended standalone funding in Dec 2024, wound down by end-2025) [S19]. Mobileye has not launched (2027 plan, ~100 vehicles initially) [S18]. Tesla's robotaxi is a small pilot: ~44 active vehicles across 7 US metros with safety monitors and ~15+ minute waits versus Waymo's ~5.7 minutes [S20]; unsupervised FSD on customer cars is delayed to Q2 2027 and confined to existing geofenced zones, California still requires safety drivers, and HW3 vehicles cannot run it [S21]. Tesla's ~$0.81/mile undercuts Waymo's $1.36–1.43/mile — a real cost edge if it can certify safety at scale [S20].

## Risks and counter-evidence
Against the Sell (bull case): net cash ≈ $35.9B ($45.4B cash and investments vs $9.5B debt), debt/equity 0.08, current ratio 2.16 [S12][S14]; FY2025 operating cash flow ~3.9x net income [S4]; automotive gross margin ex-credits improved to 18.1% from 16.3% (unverified company guidance) [S5]; energy gross margin jumped to 33.1% from 20.4% (unverified company guidance) [S5]; 59% US share [S10]; capex was cut to ~$20B from ~$25B, supporting near-term free cash flow [S22][S23][S24]; and the incumbent field is thinner than it looks — only Waymo has Western scale [S16][S18][S19].
Against a Buy (supporting the Sell): flat revenue and −43% Q3 net income [S12][S13]; ~500x trailing earnings on shrinking profits [S14]; 96.9% volume concentration in Model 3/Y [S9]; the autonomy walk-back to 2027 with a pilot far smaller than Waymo's fleet [S8][S20][S21]; and a ~22% share-count uncertainty in the market cap [S11][S12].

## Scenarios
- Bull: robotaxi/FSD monetizes in 2027, energy gross margin stays high, US dominance holds; the ~500x multiple [S14] is sustained by 2027+ optionality.
- Base: auto revenue stays flat, FSD grows gradually, operating margin holds mid-single digits; the stock derates as growth disappoints.
- Bear: share loss to BYD accelerates, robotaxi slips again, capex re-escalates; the multiple compresses toward the market.

## The one diligence question
Between now and robotaxi revenue becoming material in mid-2027, what re-accelerates revenue and operating margin enough to support a ~$1.61T market cap [S12] — or is the entire stock an option on a 2027+ autonomy story where Waymo already leads on operating scale [S16][S20]?

## Three takeaways
1. Sell: the valuation prices a growth-and-margin story the last three fiscal years do not show [S2][S3][S4][S14].
2. The balance sheet (net cash ~$35.9B) [S12][S14] argues against a distressed short, but not against derating from ~500x trailing earnings [S14].
3. The bull case now rests on 2027+ autonomy/robotics optionality, where Tesla trails Waymo on operating scale and timeline [S16][S20][S21].

- Profitability improved despite flat revenue: automotive gross margin ex-regulatory-credits rose to 18.1% (from 16.3%), energy gross margin to 33.1% (from 20.4%), with $1.5B free cash flow and $45B+ cash on hand [S5].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Memo version 3 (rating Sell, data as of 2026-10-28):

# Tesla (TSLA): investment memo
Rating: Sell
Data as of: 2026-10-28

## Executive summary
Sell. Tesla's core automotive business has stopped growing and its profitability has collapsed: GAAP net income fell from $15.0B (FY2023) to $3.79B (FY2025) [S2][S3][S4], and Q3 2026 net income of $787M was down 43% year-over-year on flat revenue [S12][S13]. The autonomy/robotaxi thesis that carries the valuation has slipped, and Tesla now trails the only scaled Western operator: unsupervised FSD is delayed to Q2 2027 and confined to geofenced zones, while Waymo is already running ~500k paid rides a week [S8][S16][S21]. The market still prices this at ~$1.61T, roughly 500x trailing earnings [S1][S12][S14]. The balance sheet is strong, so this is not a distress call; the valuation embeds growth and margins the business is not delivering. Three key facts: (1) net income fell ~75% over two fiscal years [S2][S3][S4]; (2) Q3 2026 operating margin was 2.6% [S13]; (3) Tesla holds 8.9% of global BEV sales versus BYD's 17.1% [S10].

## Business
Tesla sells EVs (Model 3 and Model Y were 96.9% of 2025 deliveries [S9]), energy generation and storage, and services (FSD subscriptions, supercharging, used vehicles, service). Q3 2026: automotive revenue $20.56B (~73% of the $28.05B total), energy $2.88B (−16% YoY, partly non-recurring tariff-related customer refunds), services & other $4.61B (+32.5%), now the second-largest segment [S6][S12]. Management claims FSD monetization is scaling — 1.7M+ paid customers, ~50% subscriptions, and >75% of North American deliveries with a paid FSD sign-up — but these are unverified company figures from the Q3 earnings call [S5]. The company is concentrated in the US, where it holds 59% of EV sales [S10].

## Financials
FY2023–FY2025 from primary filings [S2][S3][S4]; Q3 2026 from a secondary 10-Q reproduction and an independent report [S12][S13].

| FY (GAAP) | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Net income | $15.0B [S2] | $7.09B [S3] | $3.79B [S4] |

FY2025: revenue $94.83B, −2.9% YoY [S4]; operating margin 4.6% (vs 7.2% FY2024) [S14]; operating cash flow $14.75B on $8.53B capex, free cash flow ~$6.2B [S4]. Q3 2026: revenue $28.05B, flat YoY [S12][S13]; GAAP net income $787M (−43%) [S12][S13]; operating income $718M (−56%) [S13]; operating margin 2.6% [S13]; free cash flow $1.53B [S13]; regulatory credits $113M (−73% YoY) [S12][S13]. The ~75% two-year net-income decline is the reported GAAP change [S2][S4]; it reflects operating-margin compression and the regulatory-credit drop [S13][S14], but we have not verified whether one-off items in the FY2023 base exaggerate the fall. Data-quality note: the Q3 2026 statements and the 3.953B share count rest on a secondary reproduction of the 10-Q [S12] and Electrek's report [S13] rather than the raw filing; the primary 10-Q has since been retrieved [S22] and used to reconcile capex, but the Q3 segment detail should be treated as high-quality secondary, not primary.

## Valuation and price
Price $407.46, NasdaqGS, USD, as of 2026-10-27T20:00 UTC [S1]; 52-week range $298.32–$489.88 [S1]. Market cap ≈ $1.61T on 3,952,757,946 shares per the 10-Q cover [S12]. Trailing multiples: P/E ≈ 500x on TTM net income of ~$3.2B [S14]; P/S ≈ 15.6x [S14]; P/B ≈ 18x [S14]; EV/EBITDA ≈ 154x (EV ≈ $1.575T on TTM EBITDA ~$10.2B) [S12][S14][S15]. TTM EBITDA is a derived estimate; treat the multiple as approximate [S15]. Share-count caveat: one vendor reports 3.237B shares [S11] versus the 10-Q's 3.953B [S12] — a ~22% difference that would swing the implied market cap materially, so the figure should be resolved against the primary filing [S11][S12].

## Competition and market
BYD leads globally: 17.1% of global EV sales versus Tesla's 8.9% [S10]; BYD overtook Tesla in 2025 on BEV volume (2.26M vs 1.64M), revenue and net profit [S9]; Tesla's 2025 sales fell in the US (−7.7%), Europe (−38.8%) and China (−8.1%) [S9]. Global EV sales exceeded 20M in 2025 and are forecast at ~23M for 2026, but Q1 2026 was down 8% YoY on US and China policy shifts [S7].

Autonomy benchmark — Tesla is behind the only scaled Western operator. Waymo runs ~3,000 robotaxis and ~500k paid rides/week (~4M rider-only miles/week) across 11 US cities, and is targeting ~1M rides/week plus Tokyo and London by end-2026 [S16]. Baidu Apollo Go leads on disclosed ride volume but is China-only and geofenced: 3.2M fully driverless rides in Q1 2026, >22M cumulative, 27 cities, no standalone economics disclosed [S17]. Cruise exited (GM ended standalone funding in Dec 2024, wound down by end-2025) [S19]. Mobileye has not launched (2027 plan, ~100 vehicles initially) [S18]. Tesla's robotaxi is a small pilot: ~44 active vehicles across 7 US metros with safety monitors and ~15+ minute waits versus Waymo's ~5.7 minutes [S20]; unsupervised FSD on customer cars is delayed to Q2 2027 and confined to existing geofenced zones, California still requires safety drivers, and HW3 vehicles cannot run it [S21]. Tesla's ~$0.81/mile undercuts Waymo's $1.36–1.43/mile — a real cost edge if it can certify safety at scale [S20].

## Risks and counter-evidence
Against the Sell (bull case): net cash ≈ $35.9B ($45.4B cash and investments vs $9.5B debt), debt/equity 0.08, current ratio 2.16 [S12][S14]; FY2025 operating cash flow ~3.9x net income [S4]; automotive gross margin ex-credits improved to 18.1% from 16.3% (unverified company guidance) [S5]; energy gross margin jumped to 33.1% from 20.4% (unverified company guidance) [S5]; 59% US share [S10]; capex was cut to ~$20B from ~$25B, supporting near-term free cash flow [S22][S23][S24]; and the incumbent field is thinner than it looks — only Waymo has Western scale [S16][S18][S19].
Against a Buy (supporting the Sell): flat revenue and −43% Q3 net income [S12][S13]; ~500x trailing earnings on shrinking profits [S14]; 96.9% volume concentration in Model 3/Y [S9]; the autonomy walk-back to 2027 with a pilot far smaller than Waymo's fleet [S8][S20][S21]; and a ~22% share-count uncertainty in the market cap [S11][S12].

## Scenarios
- Bull: robotaxi/FSD monetizes in 2027, energy gross margin stays high, US dominance holds; the ~500x multiple [S14] is sustained by 2027+ optionality.
- Base: auto revenue stays flat, FSD grows gradually, operating margin holds mid-single digits; the stock derates as growth disappoints.
- Bear: share loss to BYD accelerates, robotaxi slips again, capex re-escalates; the multiple compresses toward the market.

## The one diligence question
Between now and robotaxi revenue becoming material in mid-2027, what re-accelerates revenue and operating margin enough to support a ~$1.61T market cap [S12] — or is the entire stock an option on a 2027+ autonomy story where Waymo already leads on operating scale [S16][S20]?

## Three takeaways
1. Sell: the valuation prices a growth-and-margin story the last three fiscal years do not show [S2][S3][S4][S14].
2. The balance sheet (net cash ~$35.9B) [S12][S14] argues against a distressed short, but not against derating from ~500x trailing earnings [S14].
3. The bull case now rests on 2027+ autonomy/robotics optionality, where Tesla trails Waymo on operating scale and timeline [S16][S20][S21].
